name: Phnom Penh
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Phnom Penh: SEZ supplier checks, garment sourcing integrity, property and partner diligence, award support.
hero_lede: Phnom Penh is Cambodia's capital, its main commercial centre and the seat of its ministries, courts and arbitration centre. TDSC helps clients research Phnom Penh partners, factories and property interests, and supports counsel in disputes and award enforcement that run through the capital's institutions.
intro: Phnom Penh sits where the Tonle Sap river meets the Mekong and is the centre of Cambodia's government, finance and services. Its industrial base is light and labour-intensive: garments, footwear, food and beverage and consumer products, much of it export-oriented. The Phnom Penh Special Economic Zone, established in 2006 and described by ASEAN Briefing as the most developed in the country, hosts manufacturers and logistics firms including well-known international brands. Tourism, hotels and a large condominium market have grown alongside manufacturing. National investment approvals are concentrated in the capital: the Council for the Development of Cambodia approved 414 projects worth about US$6.9 billion in 2024.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Phnom Penh because so much of Cambodia's foreign investment, sourcing and political-economic decision-making passes through it. Brands and buyers need to know who actually owns and controls the factories and agents they rely on. Investors in property, hospitality and financial services face opaque shareholdings, nominee arrangements and close links between business and officials. Lenders and claimants pursue assets after defaults, and arbitration parties must navigate recognition and enforcement in the capital's courts. Phnom Penh is also a point of reference for regional concerns about scam compounds, money laundering and illicit finance, which makes counterparty screening a routine requirement rather than an exception.

matters.title: Garment and footwear supplier ownership
matters.text: Establishing who owns and controls Phnom Penh garment, footwear and packaging suppliers and their subcontractors, testing claimed capacity and compliance history, and identifying links to agents or officials, for brands and buyers managing sourcing, labour and customs risk in their Cambodian supply chain.

matters.title: SEZ tenant and partner diligence
matters.text: Background research on manufacturers, logistics operators and developers in and around the Phnom Penh Special Economic Zone before a joint venture, lease or supply agreement, covering ownership chains often running through Hong Kong, China, Singapore or Thailand, adverse media and litigation.

matters.title: Real estate and hotel investments
matters.text: Reviewing developers, landholders and hotel or condominium projects in the capital, including the practical limits on foreign land ownership, nominee and long-lease structures, title history and disputes, before clients invest, lend or take a strata or leasehold interest.

matters.title: Illicit finance and scam exposure
matters.text: Screening Phnom Penh counterparties, payment processors, casinos-adjacent businesses and property owners for links to online scam operations, money laundering or sanctioned persons, for banks, payment firms and corporates conducting enhanced due diligence on Cambodian relationships.

matters.title: Asset research for award enforcement
matters.text: Locating assets of Phnom Penh-based debtors, such as company shareholdings, real property and business interests, to support counsel seeking recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards or foreign judgments through the Cambodian courts, and documenting how assets have moved.

local_context.title: Courts in the capital
local_context.text: Phnom Penh hosts the Phnom Penh Court of Appeal, one of four appellate courts in Cambodia as of 2022 alongside Sihanoukville, Battambang and Tbong Khmum, as well as the Supreme Court and the capital's court of first instance. Courts of Appeal are designed with commercial and labour chambers, but as of 2022 only civil, criminal and investigating chambers operated, so commercial disputes are heard in civil chambers. A dedicated commercial court has been under discussion for many years.

local_context.title: National Commercial Arbitration Centre
local_context.text: The National Commercial Arbitration Centre (NCAC) is Cambodia's arbitral institution. Its rules draw on the SIAC rules, and it settled its first cases around 2017. Practitioners report growing use, including domestically, and Phnom Penh is a common choice of seat. Recognition and enforcement of foreign awards goes to the Court of Appeal and can take about six months, or two to three years if appeals run their course.

local_context.title: Enforcement practicalities
local_context.text: Practitioners cite recurring obstacles in Phnom Penh enforcement proceedings: broad public order objections, arguments that parts of a foreign-law transaction must be governed by Cambodian law, local injunctions used to pull merits into court, and the requirement to translate filings into Khmer. These add time and cost, and they make early asset research and a clear evidentiary record especially valuable for creditors.

local_context.title: Ministries and investment bodies
local_context.text: The Ministry of Commerce, which runs the national online business registration system, and the Council for the Development of Cambodia, which approves qualified investment projects and oversees special economic zones, are both based in Phnom Penh. Investment approvals and SEZ data published by these bodies are a useful starting point for verifying a project's status, sponsors and claimed tax incentives.

tdsc_approach: TDSC handles Phnom Penh matters from Nashville and has no office in Cambodia. We start with what can be checked lawfully: Ministry of Commerce registration data, investment and SEZ approvals, court and arbitration records available through counsel, regional corporate registries where ownership runs offshore, and Khmer, English and Chinese-language media. Where enquiries on the ground are needed, such as factory site checks, discreet market interviews or property verification, TDSC coordinates experienced local professionals working alongside Cambodian counsel, without pretexting or access to restricted records. Given regional concerns about scam operations and illicit finance, every matter is screened for sanctions exposure, and reports separate documented facts from local reputation and inference.

faqs.q: Can the real owner of a Phnom Penh factory be identified?
faqs.a: Often, but rarely from one record. Registration data may show a local company with Cambodian shareholders, while control sits with a foreign group or an individual through nominees, leases or financing. We combine Cambodian filings with registries in Hong Kong, China, Singapore or elsewhere, trade data, media and local enquiries, and state the confidence level for each link.

faqs.q: Where is a foreign arbitral award enforced against a Phnom Penh company?
faqs.a: Recognition and enforcement applications go to the Court of Appeal, with further appeal to the Supreme Court, both in Phnom Penh. Practitioners estimate about six months at first instance and two to three years if appeals are exhausted. Counsel handles the proceedings; TDSC can support with asset research and background on the debtor and its controllers.

faqs.q: Is there a commercial court in Phnom Penh?
faqs.a: As of the most recent sources we reviewed, commercial disputes are heard by civil chambers because dedicated commercial chambers had not been established, and a separate commercial court has long been planned. Clients should confirm the current position with Cambodian counsel, as reform proposals have been advanced and the structure may change.

faqs.q: How do you approach property due diligence in Phnom Penh?
faqs.a: Foreign investors usually hold Cambodian property through strata title in qualifying buildings, long leases or local structures, each with its own risks. We review the developer and landholder, title history and disputes through counsel and local professionals, and check for links to politically exposed or sanctioned persons before an investment or loan.

faqs.q: Why do banks ask for enhanced diligence on Phnom Penh counterparties?
faqs.a: Cambodia features in international reporting on online scam compounds, money laundering and related sanctions actions, and some activity is linked to businesses in or around the capital. Enhanced diligence helps establish whether a counterparty, its owners or its premises have such links. We report what public and lawfully obtained sources show, without speculation.
